candidates.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
candidates.author: Virginia Woolf
candidates.locator: chapter one, closing the Oxbridge luncheon and the Fernham dinner (Hogarth Press, 1929)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It puts the body’s plain needs under every claim about what people owe one another: the mind cannot do its work unfed, so a fair share of the dinner is where justice begins.

candidates.quote: If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world.
candidates.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
candidates.locator: chapter XVIII, The Return Journey (George Allen and Unwin, 1937)
candidates.speaker: Thorin Oakenshield
candidates.whyThisMonth: It sets the things that are shared out, food and cheer and song, above the thing that is kept, and says which of the two makes the better world to wake into.

candidates.quote: To tame the Proud, the fetter’d Slave to free; / These are Imperial Arts, and worthy thee.
candidates.author: Virgil
candidates.locator: Book VI, lines 1177 to 1178 in Dryden (Latin 6.853), The Works of Virgil (Jacob Tonson, 1697)
candidates.speaker: Anchises
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the oldest plain statement of what power owes anyone under it: humble the proud, free the fettered, and count nothing else worth the name of an art.

candidates.quote: Why is it always the innocents who suffer most, when you high lords play your game of thrones?
candidates.author: George R. R. Martin
candidates.speaker: Varys, to Eddard Stark
candidates.whyThisMonth: It asks the question the month exists to answer, which is who actually pays when the powerful play, and it asks it of the decent man rather than the wicked one.

candidates.quote: I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain.
candidates.author: Ernest Hemingway
candidates.speaker: Frederic Henry
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is a warning against the big words that get spent on other people’s behalf, and a demand for plain speech about what is actually being asked of them.

candidates.quote: What is the chief end of man?—to get rich. In what way?—dishonestly if we can; honestly if we must.
candidates.author: Mark Twain
candidates.locator: the opening question and answer, New York Tribune, 27 September 1871
candidates.whyThisMonth: Twain writes out the creed that a month on justice has to answer, and hearing it said flatly at six in the morning is what makes the answering feel urgent.
